tasks.currentSketch: If f(a)=f(b)=k and f is constant, its derivative is zero throughout (a,b). Otherwise f takes a value above or below k. In the above case, continuity on [a,b] gives an absolute maximum; it cannot occur at an endpoint, so it occurs at an interior point and Fermat’s theorem gives f′(c)=0. The below case uses an interior minimum.

tasks.currentSketch: Let ℓ be the line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)), with slope m=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a), and set g=f−ℓ. Then g(a)=g(b)=0 and g inherits continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b). Rolle’s theorem gives g′(c)=0, hence f′(c)=m.

tasks.currentSketch: Use the telescoping identity 1/n²=Σ_{k=n}∞(1/k−1/(k+1))? This identity is false (the RHS equals 1/n). So that is not a valid proof route. A valid trigonometric telescoping route uses cotangent partial fractions: cot x=1/x−2xΣₙ≥1(1/(n²π²−x²)); compare x-coefficients near 0 with cot x=1/x−x/3+… to obtain Σ1/n²=π²/6.
